360	They know that each of us looks for his place
361	in the world. What is "his place"? A place where he feels good,
362	a place that suits him. Not every place suits everyone.
363	Rabbi Nachman says: there is a place designated for good
364	and blessing, and the opposite as well. And when a person is in his place, it is
365	a completely different world. We all know what it feels like
366	to be in your own home, to be in a place
367	that you know and love and are loved, feel good, feel
368	comfortable. You love the view, you love the atmosphere,
369	you love the weather, you love
370	the design of the house, you love the neighborhood. And we all
371	know how a person feels when he is in a place that doesn't suit him: he doesn't like the atmosphere, he
372	doesn't like the weather, he doesn't like
373	the people, he doesn't like the design of the house. It
374	weighs on him, it doesn't let him breathe. And this is something
375	that seems to be only
376	physical. So each one looks for his place in the world.
377	Each one looks for his friends. Each one looks for
378	where the people are
379	that I will be with in love, in connection and in affection, and who
380	will help me. Rabbi Nachman writes in Sefer HaMidot: whoever
381	has no friends and loved ones, it is better for him to die. It is
382	more comfortable to die than
383	to live cut off, with no one at all who cares about me, no
384	one who knows me and takes an interest in me. This is a
385	need of a person: where are my friends? I want to find
386	them. And each one has guides. Each one has
387	people who can give him direction, give him
388	help. Where are my guides? Where are
389	my leaders?
390	And each one of us looks for his occupation. What
391	is the profession? What do I need to do in life? Not only
392	for
393	a livelihood. Even someone who has a livelihood and is settled
394	in some way, because he is helped, he has some
395	inheritance, he needs to engage in something. He feels
396	a need to engage in something. What will I engage in? What is the field
397	of my occupation? He doesn't know. He looks for
398	it. And we are still talking about external things,
399	but there are also inner things. Where is my joy?
400	My joy. Many times a person has things,
401	looks and says: I should be happy, I have
402	good things in life, why am I not happy? Where
403	is my joy? What keeps me from
404	being happy? Many times a person says: I'm not happy,
405	I have troubles, I have problems. And it is so
406	frustrating to discover that even when the troubles and problems
407	calm down, and even when there are good things, you are not
408	able
409	to be happy. Where is my joy? I have some
410	capacity to be happy. Where is it? Where is this thing?
411	Where is this
412	thing? Where is my success? Where will I succeed? Where
413	is my special purpose? What is my matter
414	in life? What do I need to do?
415	And of course each one looks for: where is my soulmate? Where is
416	my other half, who will complete me, with whom I
417	will build a life? These are so many very, very important things:
418	my place, my friends, my partner in life,
419	my teachers,
420	my joy, my purpose. Where is my holiness?
421	Where is my wholeness? All these things, where are they?
422	It is not...
423	It is as if it is found
424	somewhere. It is mine, but someone took it from me.
425	Someone stole it from me. Whether it is since Adam
426	HaRishon, or since I did some foolish thing
427	or other, or I don't even know why, I don't
428	remember why. But where are these things?
429	To find what belongs to me, to find what
430	I lost. Rabbi Nachman calls this
431	teshuvah, because the word teshuvah means to return,
432	to go back to what belongs to you. Return, return
433	home. Return to your loved ones, return to your place,
434	to your joy, to your direction, to your purpose. Return. But
435	we know that the word
436	teshuvah
437	means regret for a sin. So how does it fit that Rabbi
438	Nachman says that returning to your place is in fact, the Zohar
439	says, this is
440	teshuvah? After all, teshuvah is to fix my transgressions,
441	to fix my mistakes, to fix my sins.
442	There really is a connection, because I cannot return
443	to my place since something is getting in the way and preventing me. What
444	gets in the way and prevents me is my mistakes and my transgressions
445	and the things I did not do as I should have. I need
446	to fix them. I need to clear the ground so
447	that I can return. I cannot return because
448	the road is blocked. I blocked it. So to return
449	in teshuvah is to clear the road and return to my place. It is
450	actually the same
451	thing.
452	The sins of a person, his mistakes, cause
453	a kitrug. Kitrug means that there is a court in heaven,
454	that in the courts above they decide what will happen here
455	in the world, and there is someone sitting there who says, or several
456	like that, about this person: he doesn't deserve, he doesn't deserve
457	good, he doesn't deserve joy, he doesn't deserve a spouse, he doesn't
458	deserve a home, according to his behavior he doesn't deserve
459	it. If I remove the kitrug, then the
460	road will open. I will find my soulmate, I will find
461	the home, I will find the livelihood, the
462	abundance, the health, everything I want. I need to remove the
463	kitrug. Simply, to remove the kitrug means
464	to regret my mistakes and to fix
465	my ways. Baruch HaShem, we do this. We
466	do this, each one of us tries to improve.
467	But because we don't know exactly how
468	to do it, we don't know exactly what
469	we spoiled and exactly how to fix it, it is not so
470	quick to succeed in moving the
471	kitrug. So we have another piece of advice,
472	a parallel one, to move and remove the kitrug that says: you
473	will not reach what suits you, what you need.
474	And this
475	advice is to wait.
476	To wait. Rabbi Natan writes: because of the sin of Adam
477	HaRishon, and likewise each one through his sin, it is impossible
478	to draw near immediately. That is, Rabbi Nachman comes and innovates
